title.en: Linear Transformations, Matrix Representations & Change of Basis

body.en: A function between vector spaces that respects addition and scalar multiplication is called a linear transformation. While Chapter 3 introduced matrix–vector multiplication as an algebraic operation, this chapter reveals the deeper geometric reality: every linear operator on finite-dimensional spaces is intrinsically represented by a matrix once bases are chosen. Linear transformations form the conceptual bridge connecting abstract vector spaces, geometry, and linear operator theory across quantum mechanics, computer graphics, and continuous dynamical systems.

Let \( V \) and \( W \) be vector spaces over \( \mathbb{R} \). A mapping \( T: V \to W \) is a linear transformation (or linear operator when \( V = W \)) if and only if for all vectors \( \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V \) and every scalar \( c \in \mathbb{R} \):

  1. Additivity: \( T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v}) \)
  2. Scalar Homogeneity: \( T(c\mathbf{u}) = c\,T(\mathbf{u}) \)

These two conditions are equivalent to the single superposition condition: \[ T(c_1\mathbf{u} + c_2\mathbf{v}) = c_1 T(\mathbf{u}) + c_2 T(\mathbf{v}) \] for all scalars \( c_1, c_2 \). By induction, a linear map preserves arbitrary linear combinations: \[ T\left(\sum_{i=1}^k c_i \mathbf{v}_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i T(\mathbf{v}_i). \]

Zero Vector Property: Taking \( c = 0 \) yields \( T(\mathbf{0}_V) = T(0 \cdot \mathbf{0}_V) = 0 \cdot T(\mathbf{0}_V) = \mathbf{0}_W \). Every linear map strictly maps the origin of the domain to the origin of the codomain. Any mapping with \( T(\mathbf{0}) \neq \mathbf{0} \) (such as the affine shift \( f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b} \) with \( \mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{0} \)) is not linear.

label.en: ▲ Level 1 Foundation — Theorem 7.1: The Standard Matrix Representation

body.en: Let \( T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m \) be a linear transformation. Then there exists a unique \( m \times n \) matrix \( [T] \) (or \( A \)), called the standard matrix of \( T \), such that: \[ T(\mathbf{x}) = [T]\mathbf{x} \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n. \] Furthermore, the columns of \( [T] \) are precisely the images of the standard basis vectors \( \mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{e}_n \) of \( \mathbb{R}^n \): \[ [T] = \begin{pmatrix} | & | & & | \\ T(\mathbf{e}_1) & T(\mathbf{e}_2) & \cdots & T(\mathbf{e}_n) \\ | & | & & | \end{pmatrix}. \]

Any vector \( \mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)^T \in \mathbb{R}^n \) can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of standard basis vectors: \[ \mathbf{x} = x_1\mathbf{e}_1 + x_2\mathbf{e}_2 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{e}_n = \sum_{j=1}^n x_j \mathbf{e}_j. \] Applying the linear transformation \( T \) and utilizing linearity across the summation and scalar coefficients: \[ T(\mathbf{x}) = T\left( \sum_{j=1}^n x_j \mathbf{e}_j \right) = \sum_{j=1}^n x_j T(\mathbf{e}_j). \] By the fundamental definition of matrix–vector multiplication (a linear combination of the matrix columns weighted by the vector components): \[ \sum_{j=1}^n x_j T(\mathbf{e}_j) = \begin{pmatrix} | & | & & | \\ T(\mathbf{e}_1) & T(\mathbf{e}_2) & \cdots & T(\mathbf{e}_n) \\ | & | & & | \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end{pmatrix} = [T]\mathbf{x}. \] Uniqueness follows from evaluating \( T(\mathbf{e}_j) \): if \( A\mathbf{x} = B\mathbf{x} \) for all \( \mathbf{x} \), setting \( \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{e}_j \) yields \( A\mathbf{e}_j = B\mathbf{e}_j \), forcing the \( j \)-th columns of \( A \) and \( B \) to be identical for all \( j \). Hence \( [T] \) is unique. \( \blacksquare \)

label.en: Worked Example 7.A (Level 1) — Canonical Geometric Operators in ℝ²

body.en:
Construct the standard transformation matrices for three foundational geometric operators on \( \mathbb{R}^2 \):

  1. Counterclockwise Rotation by Angle \( \theta \) (\( R_\theta \)):
    Under rotation by \( \theta \), \( \mathbf{e}_1 = (1, 0)^T \mapsto (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)^T \) and \( \mathbf{e}_2 = (0, 1)^T \mapsto (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)^T \).
    Therefore: \[ [R_\theta] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}. \]
  2. Reflection Across a Line Through the Origin at Angle \( \alpha \) (\( M_\alpha \)):
    Unit vector along the line is \( \mathbf{u} = (\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)^T \). Reflection maps \( \mathbf{x} \mapsto 2(\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{u})\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{x} \). Evaluating on standard basis vectors: \[ [M_\alpha] = \begin{pmatrix} \cos(2\alpha) & \sin(2\alpha) \\ \sin(2\alpha) & -\cos(2\alpha) \end{pmatrix}. \]
  3. Horizontal Shear by Factor \( k \) (\( S_k \)):
    \( S_k(x, y) = (x + ky, y) \). Here \( S_k(\mathbf{e}_1) = (1, 0)^T \) and \( S_k(\mathbf{e}_2) = (k, 1)^T \), giving: \[ [S_k] = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & k \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

label.en: ● Level 2 Analytical Application — Definition 7.2: Kernel, Image & Morphisms

body.en:
For any linear transformation \( T: V \to W \):

  • Kernel (Null Space): The set of all input vectors mapped to the zero vector in \( W \): \[ \ker(T) = \operatorname{null}(T) = \{ \mathbf{v} \in V : T(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}_W \}. \] \( \ker(T) \) is a vector subspace of the domain \( V \). Its dimension is the nullity of \( T \): \( \operatorname{nullity}(T) = \dim(\ker T) \).
  • Image (Range): The set of all output vectors achievable in \( W \): \[ \operatorname{im}(T) = \operatorname{range}(T) = \{ \mathbf{w} \in W : \exists \mathbf{v} \in V \text{ such that } T(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{w} \}. \] \( \operatorname{im}(T) \) is a vector subspace of the codomain \( W \), equivalent to the column space \( \operatorname{Col}([T]) \). Its dimension is the rank of \( T \): \( \operatorname{rank}(T) = \dim(\operatorname{im} T) \).
  • Injectivity (One-to-One): \( T \) is injective if \( T(\mathbf{u}) = T(\mathbf{v}) \implies \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v} \).
  • Surjectivity (Onto): \( T \) is surjective if \( \operatorname{im}(T) = W \) (i.e., \( \operatorname{rank}(T) = \dim(W) \)).
  • Isomorphism (Bijective): \( T \) is an isomorphism if it is both injective and surjective. In this case, \( V \) and \( W \) are isomorphic (\( V \cong W \)), which requires \( \dim(V) = \dim(W) \).

label.en: ▲ Level 2 Analytical Application — Theorem 7.2: Injectivity and the Trivial Kernel

body.en: Let \( T: V \to W \) be a linear transformation. Then \( T \) is injective (one-to-one) if and only if \( \ker(T) = \{ \mathbf{0}_V \} \) (i.e., \( \operatorname{nullity}(T) = 0 \)).

Forward Direction (\( \implies \)): Assume \( T \) is injective. We already know \( T(\mathbf{0}_V) = \mathbf{0}_W \), so \( \mathbf{0}_V \in \ker(T) \). Now let \( \mathbf{v} \in \ker(T) \). Then \( T(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}_W \). Thus \( T(\mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{0}_V) \). Because \( T \) is injective, this directly implies \( \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}_V \). Hence, \( \ker(T) = \{ \mathbf{0}_V \} \).

Reverse Direction (\( \impliedby \)): Assume \( \ker(T) = \{ \mathbf{0}_V \} \). Suppose \( T(\mathbf{u}) = T(\mathbf{v}) \) for some \( \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V \). Subtracting \( T(\mathbf{v}) \) from both sides and applying linearity gives: \[ T(\mathbf{u}) - T(\mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}_W. \] By definition of the kernel, \( \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \in \ker(T) \). Since \( \ker(T) = \{ \mathbf{0}_V \} \), we must have \( \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}_V \), which means \( \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v} \). Therefore, \( T \) is one-to-one. \( \blacksquare \)

label.en: ▲ Level 2 Analytical Application — Theorem 7.3: The Dimension Theorem for Linear Maps

body.en: If \( V \) is a finite-dimensional vector space and \( T: V \to W \) is a linear transformation, then: \[ \dim(\ker T) + \dim(\operatorname{im} T) = \dim(V), \] or equivalently: \[ \operatorname{nullity}(T) + \operatorname{rank}(T) = \dim(V). \]

Let \( n = \dim(V) \) and let \( k = \dim(\ker T) \). If \( k = 0 \), the kernel is \( \{ \mathbf{0} \} \) with basis \( \emptyset \). Otherwise, choose a basis \( \mathcal{B}_K = \{ \mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_k \} \) for \( \ker(T) \).

By the Basis Extension Theorem, extend \( \mathcal{B}_K \) to a complete basis for \( V \): \[ \mathcal{B} = \{ \mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{w}_{n-k} \}. \] We claim that the set \( \mathcal{S} = \{ T(\mathbf{w}_1), T(\mathbf{w}_2), \ldots, T(\mathbf{w}_{n-k}) \} \) is a basis for \( \operatorname{im}(T) \).

1. \( \mathcal{S} \) spans \( \operatorname{im}(T) \): Let \( \mathbf{y} \in \operatorname{im}(T) \). Then \( \mathbf{y} = T(\mathbf{v}) \) for some \( \mathbf{v} \in V \). Express \( \mathbf{v} \) in terms of \( \mathcal{B} \): \[ \mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i \mathbf{u}_i + \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} d_j \mathbf{w}_j. \] Applying \( T \) and noting \( T(\mathbf{u}_i) = \mathbf{0} \) for all \( i \): \[ \mathbf{y} = T(\mathbf{v}) = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i T(\mathbf{u}_i) + \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} d_j T(\mathbf{w}_j) = \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} d_j T(\mathbf{w}_j). \] Thus \( \operatorname{span}(\mathcal{S}) = \operatorname{im}(T) \).

2. \( \mathcal{S} \) is linearly independent: Suppose \[ \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} d_j T(\mathbf{w}_j) = \mathbf{0}_W. \] By linearity, \( T\left( \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} d_j \mathbf{w}_j \right) = \mathbf{0}_W \), which proves that the vector \( \mathbf{w} = \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} d_j \mathbf{w}_j \) lies in \( \ker(T) \). Since \( \mathcal{B}_K \) is a basis for \( \ker(T) \), \( \mathbf{w} \) can be written as: \[ \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} d_j \mathbf{w}_j = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i \mathbf{u}_i \iff \sum_{i=1}^k (-c_i)\mathbf{u}_i + \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} d_j \mathbf{w}_j = \mathbf{0}_V. \] Because the combined set \( \mathcal{B} \) is linearly independent in \( V \), all coefficients must vanish: \( c_1 = \cdots = c_k = d_1 = \cdots = d_{n-k} = 0 \). In particular, \( d_1 = d_2 = \cdots = d_{n-k} = 0 \), establishing that \( \mathcal{S} \) is linearly independent.

Since \( \mathcal{S} \) spans \( \operatorname{im}(T) \) and is linearly independent, it is a basis for \( \operatorname{im}(T) \). Hence \( \dim(\operatorname{im} T) = n - k = \dim(V) - \dim(\ker T) \), completing the proof. \( \blacksquare \)

label.en: Worked Example 7.B (Level 2) — Dimension Theorem & Kernel Computation

body.en:
Consider the linear transformation \( T: \mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}^3 \) defined by \( T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} \) where: \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 & 4 & 8 \end{pmatrix}. \] Determine a basis for \( \ker(T) \), a basis for \( \operatorname{im}(T) \), and verify the Dimension Theorem.

Step 1: Row reduce \( A \) to RREF: \[ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 & 4 & 8 \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow{R_2 - 2R_1,\, R_3 - 4R_1} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 & -4 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 & -4 \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow{R_3 - R_2,\, R_2 / 4} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \xrightarrow{R_1 + R_2} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Step 2: Basis for \( \ker(T) \): Pivot variables are \( x_1, x_2 \); free variables are \( x_3 = s, x_4 = t \). Expressing pivot variables: \( x_1 = -s - 2t \) and \( x_2 = s + t \). In parametric vector form: \[ \mathbf{x} = s \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + t \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. \] Thus a basis for \( \ker(T) \) is \( \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \right\} \), and \( \operatorname{nullity}(T) = 2 \).

Step 3: Basis for \( \operatorname{im}(T) \): Pivot columns are columns 1 and 2 of the original matrix \( A \): \[ \text{Basis for } \operatorname{im}(T) = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \right\}, \quad \operatorname{rank}(T) = 2. \]

Verification: \( \operatorname{nullity}(T) + \operatorname{rank}(T) = 2 + 2 = 4 = \dim(\text{domain } \mathbb{R}^4) \). ✓

label.en: ● Level 3 University Rigor — Definition 7.3: Matrix Relative to Arbitrary Bases

body.en:
Let \( V \) and \( W \) be vector spaces with ordered bases \( \mathcal{B} = \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n \} \) and \( \mathcal{C} = \{ \mathbf{w}_1, \mathbf{w}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{w}_m \} \), respectively. Let \( [\mathbf{v}]_\mathcal{B} \) denote the coordinate vector of \( \mathbf{v} \) relative to \( \mathcal{B} \).

The matrix representation of \( T: V \to W \) relative to bases \( \mathcal{B} \) and \( \mathcal{C} \), denoted \( [T]_\mathcal{B}^\mathcal{C} \) (or simply \( [T]_\mathcal{B} \) when \( V = W \) and \( \mathcal{B} = \mathcal{C} \)), is the \( m \times n \) matrix whose \( j \)-th column is the coordinate vector of \( T(\mathbf{v}_j) \) with respect to \( \mathcal{C} \): \[ [T]_\mathcal{B}^\mathcal{C} = \begin{pmatrix} | & | & & | \\ [T(\mathbf{v}_1)]_\mathcal{C} & [T(\mathbf{v}_2)]_\mathcal{C} & \cdots & [T(\mathbf{v}_n)]_\mathcal{C} \\ | & | & & | \end{pmatrix}. \] This matrix satisfies the commutative diagram property: \[ [T(\mathbf{x})]_\mathcal{C} = [T]_\mathcal{B}^\mathcal{C} [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B} \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x} \in V. \]

label.en: ▲ Level 3 University Rigor — Theorem 7.4: Change of Basis & Similarity Transformations

body.en:
Let \( T: V \to V \) be a linear operator on an \( n \)-dimensional space \( V \), and let \( \mathcal{B} \) and \( \mathcal{C} \) be two ordered bases of \( V \). Let \( P = P_{\mathcal{B} \leftarrow \mathcal{C}} \) be the change-of-basis transition matrix from \( \mathcal{C} \) to \( \mathcal{B} \), whose columns are \( [\mathbf{w}_j]_\mathcal{B} \) for \( \mathbf{w}_j \in \mathcal{C} \).

Then \( P \) is invertible, \( [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B} = P [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{C} \), and the matrices representing \( T \) under \( \mathcal{B} \) and \( \mathcal{C} \) are related by a similarity transformation: \[ [T]_\mathcal{C} = P^{-1} [T]_\mathcal{B} P. \]

Similarity Invariants: Because \( [T]_\mathcal{C} \) and \( [T]_\mathcal{B} \) are similar matrices (\( B = P^{-1}AP \)), they share identical intrinsic geometric properties independent of the chosen coordinate basis:

  1. \( \det([T]_\mathcal{C}) = \det([T]_\mathcal{B}) \)
  2. \( \operatorname{tr}([T]_\mathcal{C}) = \operatorname{tr}([T]_\mathcal{B}) \)
  3. \( p_{[T]_\mathcal{C}}(\lambda) = p_{[T]_\mathcal{B}}(\lambda) \) (identical characteristic polynomial and eigenvalues)
  4. Identical rank and nullity

Let \( \mathbf{x} \in V \). By definition of the transition matrix, coordinates convert via: \[ [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B} = P [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{C} \iff [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{C} = P^{-1} [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B}. \] Applying this conversion rule to the transformed vector \( T(\mathbf{x}) \): \[ [T(\mathbf{x})]_\mathcal{C} = P^{-1} [T(\mathbf{x})]_\mathcal{B}. \] Substituting the definition \( [T(\mathbf{x})]_\mathcal{B} = [T]_\mathcal{B} [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B} \): \[ [T(\mathbf{x})]_\mathcal{C} = P^{-1} \left( [T]_\mathcal{B} [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{B} \right) = P^{-1} [T]_\mathcal{B} \left( P [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{C} \right) = \left( P^{-1} [T]_\mathcal{B} P \right) [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{C}. \] Since this equality holds for all coordinate vectors \( [\mathbf{x}]_\mathcal{C} \in \mathbb{R}^n \), uniqueness of the matrix representation establishes: \[ [T]_\mathcal{C} = P^{-1} [T]_\mathcal{B} P. \quad \blacksquare \]

label.en: Worked Example 7.C (Level 3) — Differential Operator Representation in Polynomial Spaces

body.en:
Let \( \mathcal{P}_2 \) be the vector space of real polynomials of degree at most 2. Let \( D: \mathcal{P}_2 \to \mathcal{P}_2 \) be the linear differential operator \( D(p(x)) = x p'(x) - 2 p(x) \).

  1. Find the matrix representation \( [D]_\mathcal{B} \) relative to the standard monomial basis \( \mathcal{B} = \{ 1, x, x^2 \} \).
  2. Find \( \ker(D) \) and \( \operatorname{im}(D) \), and determine whether \( D \) is an isomorphism.

Step 1: Compute images of basis elements:

  • For \( p_1(x) = 1 \): \( D(1) = x(0) - 2(1) = -2 = -2(1) + 0(x) + 0(x^2) \implies [D(1)]_\mathcal{B} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \).
  • For \( p_2(x) = x \): \( D(x) = x(1) - 2(x) = -x = 0(1) - 1(x) + 0(x^2) \implies [D(x)]_\mathcal{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \).
  • For \( p_3(x) = x^2 \): \( D(x^2) = x(2x) - 2(x^2) = 0 = 0(1) + 0(x) + 0(x^2) \implies [D(x^2)]_\mathcal{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \).

Assembling the columns into the matrix representation: \[ [D]_\mathcal{B} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Step 2: Kernel and Image Analysis:
The matrix has a pivot in columns 1 and 2, while column 3 is a free column. The null space of \( [D]_\mathcal{B} \) is spanned by \( (0, 0, 1)^T \), corresponding to the polynomial \( x^2 \).
Therefore: \[ \ker(D) = \operatorname{span}\{ x^2 \}, \quad \dim(\ker D) = 1. \] Since \( \ker(D) \neq \{0\} \), \( D \) is not injective, and by Rank-Nullity \( \operatorname{rank}(D) = 3 - 1 = 2 < 3 \) (not surjective). Hence \( D \) is not an isomorphism.
The image is spanned by \( \{ p_1, p_2 \} \): \( \operatorname{im}(D) = \operatorname{span}\{ 1, x \} \).

label.en: ⚠️ Common Traps & University Pitfalls — Linear Transformations

body.en:
• Affine Shifts are NOT Linear: A common exam trap is mistaking \( T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b} \) (for \( \mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{0} \)) for a linear transformation. Because \( T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{0} \), additivity and scalar scaling fail completely. It is an affine map, never a linear transformation.
  • Codomain Dimension vs. Range Dimension: If \( T: \mathbb{R}^5 \to \mathbb{R}^3 \), students frequently confuse the codomain \( \mathbb{R}^3 \) with \( \operatorname{im}(T) \). The dimension of the range is \( \operatorname{rank}(T) \le 3 \); \( T \) is onto only if \( \operatorname{rank}(T) = 3 \).
  • Inverting the Transition Matrix Direction: In changing basis with \( [T]_\mathcal{C} = P^{-1} [T]_\mathcal{B} P \), the transition matrix \( P = P_{\mathcal{B} \leftarrow \mathcal{C}} \) has columns given by the coordinates of the new basis \( \mathcal{C} \) relative to the old basis \( \mathcal{B} \). Swapping \( P \) and \( P^{-1} \) flips the entire coordinate perspective.
  • Composition Order: The composite transformation \( (S \circ T)(\mathbf{x}) = S(T(\mathbf{x})) \) corresponds to matrix product \( [S][T] \), applied from right to left. Reversing this product to \( [T][S] \) computes \( T \circ S \), which is generally completely distinct or undefined when dimensions differ.

caption.en: Geometric effect of the rotation transformation \( T(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{x} \). The standard basis vector \( \mathbf{e}_1 = \langle 1, 0 \rangle \) maps to \( \langle 0, 1 \rangle \), rotating the plane \( 90^\circ \) counterclockwise.

body.en:
\( T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2 \) projects every vector onto the \( x \)-axis: \( T(x,y)=(x,0) \). (a) Verify \( T \) is linear and find its standard matrix \( [T] \). (b) Find \( \ker(T) \) and \( \operatorname{im}(T) \), and verify the Dimension Theorem. (c) Explain geometrically and algebraically why \( [T] \) cannot be invertible.

Show solution

(a) \( T(c_1(x_1, y_1) + c_2(x_2, y_2)) = T(c_1 x_1 + c_2 x_2, c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2) = (c_1 x_1 + c_2 x_2, 0) = c_1(x_1, 0) + c_2(x_2, 0) = c_1 T(x_1, y_1) + c_2 T(x_2, y_2) \) — strictly linear. Testing standard basis: \( T(1,0)=(1,0) \) and \( T(0,1)=(0,0) \), hence \( [T] = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \).

(b) \( T(x,y) = (0,0) \iff x = 0 \). Thus \( \ker(T) = \{ (0, y) : y \in \mathbb{R} \} = \operatorname{span}\big((0,1)^T\big) \), which is the \( y \)-axis (\( \dim = 1 \)). The range is \( \operatorname{im}(T) = \{ (x, 0) : x \in \mathbb{R} \} = \operatorname{span}\big((1,0)^T\big) \), which is the \( x \)-axis (\( \dim = 1 \)).
Check: \( \dim(\ker T) + \dim(\operatorname{im} T) = 1 + 1 = 2 = \dim(\mathbb{R}^2) \). ✓

(c) Algebraically, \( \det([T]) = (1)(0) - (0)(0) = 0 \), so \( [T] \) is singular. Geometrically, projection permanently collapses the entire 2D plane onto a 1D line; all information along the \( y \)-axis is lost (\( \ker T \neq \{0\} \)), so the operation is non-injective and cannot be uniquely reversed.

Let \( T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2 \) be reflection across the line \( y = 2x \). Find \( [T]_\mathcal{B} \) relative to the basis \( \mathcal{B} = \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \} \) where \( \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} \) lies on the line and \( \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \) is orthogonal to the line.

Solution: Since \( \mathbf{v}_1 \) lies along the reflection line, \( T(\mathbf{v}_1) = \mathbf{v}_1 = 1\mathbf{v}_1 + 0\mathbf{v}_2 \implies [T(\mathbf{v}_1)]_\mathcal{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \).
Since \( \mathbf{v}_2 \) is perpendicular to the line, reflection negates it: \( T(\mathbf{v}_2) = -\mathbf{v}_2 = 0\mathbf{v}_1 - 1\mathbf{v}_2 \implies [T(\mathbf{v}_2)]_\mathcal{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \).
Therefore: \[ [T]_\mathcal{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. \] (Notice how selecting an eigenbasis completely diagonalizes the geometric transformation!)

Can a linear transformation \( T: \mathbb{R}^5 \to \mathbb{R}^3 \) be injective (one-to-one)? Can it be surjective (onto)?

Solution: By the Dimension Theorem, \( \dim(\ker T) + \dim(\operatorname{im} T) = 5 \). Since \( \operatorname{im}(T) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 \), \( \dim(\operatorname{im} T) \le 3 \). Thus: \[ \dim(\ker T) = 5 - \dim(\operatorname{im} T) \ge 5 - 3 = 2. \] Since \( \dim(\ker T) \ge 2 > 0 \), \( \ker(T) \neq \{\mathbf{0}\} \), so \( T \) cannot be one-to-one under any circumstances. However, if \( \operatorname{rank}(T) = 3 = \dim(\mathbb{R}^3) \), \( T \) can be surjective.

label.en: Worked Example D — Euclidean Distance & Orthogonal Projection

body.en:
A displacement has horizontal component \( \Delta x = 5 \) and vertical component \( \Delta y = 5 \). Find the squared magnitude \( d^2 \) and the area of the right triangle formed with the axes.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. By the Pythagorean theorem, \( d^2 = (5)^2 + (5)^2 = 25 + 25 = \mathbf{50} \).
  2. The enclosed right-triangle area is \( A = \frac{1}{2}(5)(5) = \mathbf{12.5} \).

question.en: A linear transformation \( T: \mathbb{R}^7 \to \mathbb{R}^4 \) has \( \dim(\ker T) = 3 \). What is the dimension of the range of \( T \), and is \( T \) surjective?

solution.en: By the Dimension Theorem, \( \operatorname{nullity}(T) + \operatorname{rank}(T) = \dim(\text{domain}) \). Here: \[ 3 + \operatorname{rank}(T) = 7 \implies \operatorname{rank}(T) = \dim(\operatorname{im} T) = 4. \] Since \( \operatorname{dim}(\operatorname{im} T) = 4 = \dim(\mathbb{R}^4) \), the range spans the entire codomain, so \( T \) is surjective (onto).

question.en: Find the standard matrix \( [T] \) of the linear operator \( T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2 \) that first rotates vectors by \( 90^\circ \) counterclockwise, and then reflects the result across the line \( y = x \).

solution.en:
Step 1: Track images of standard basis vectors:
For \( \mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \): Rotation by \( 90^\circ \) CCW sends \( \mathbf{e}_1 \) to \( \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \). Reflection across \( y = x \) swaps coordinates: \( \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \).
For \( \mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \): Rotation by \( 90^\circ \) CCW sends \( \mathbf{e}_2 \) to \( \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \). Reflection across \( y = x \) swaps coordinates: \( \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \).

Step 2: Assemble standard matrix: The columns of \( [T] \) are \( T(\mathbf{e}_1) \) and \( T(\mathbf{e}_2) \): \[ [T] = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. \] Alternatively, via matrix multiplication of standard operators: \[ [T] = [M_{\pi/4}] [R_{\pi/2}] = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. \] This composite operator is geometrically equivalent to reflection across the x-axis!

question.en: [Linear Transformations, Matrix Representations & Change of Basis · Practice 3] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 5t + 5 \), evaluate \( g(8) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 50 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 8 \): \( g(8) = 5(8) + 5 = \mathbf{45} \). Setting \( 5t + 5 = 50 \) gives \( 5t = 45 \implies t = \mathbf{9} \).

question.en: [Linear Transformations, Matrix Representations & Change of Basis · Practice 4] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 6t + 6 \), evaluate \( g(10) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 72 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 10 \): \( g(10) = 6(10) + 6 = \mathbf{66} \). Setting \( 6t + 6 = 72 \) gives \( 6t = 66 \implies t = \mathbf{11} \).
